texts.0: Why are Roman numerals written the way they are? It probably won’t surprise you to learn that no one really knows, but here are two popular ideas. Which do you believe? One is that they represent notches on a stick and the person doing the counting would make a second cut when the fifth item was reached. This became the symbol V. At ten, a further two notches were cut, forming X, and so on. Another idea is that V stands for the angle made by the thumb and little finger of your hand. The X of ten is made when you put the heels of your palms together.
texts.1: Science is about looking at the world and asking questions about it. Whether you find the answers to those questions depends upon how well you test your ideas. Once you have something interesting to ask, you need to predict what you think the answer will be. You then need to plan an experiment that tests your ideas fairly. That means that you have to consider all the possible reasons why something might happen. You should then find a way to separate all those other factors and keep them constant. That will mean that any change you see can only have one explanation.
texts.2: If you like reading books, then you have much to thank William Caxton for. He didn’t invent printing, but he was the first person to set up a printing press in England in 1472. Before this, people had to copy out books and documents by hand. This was a very skilled and difficult task. It also took a lot of time, which made it expensive. Printing meant that books could be produced more cheaply and in greater numbers. It was a major step forward in getting the country reading. We can only imagine what he would have thought of today’s word processors and printers.
texts.3: Russia is a huge country. It stretches from eastern Europe all the way to the Pacific Ocean. In fact, it is only 55 miles from the United States at one point. They are separated by a narrow stretch of water called the Bering Strait. This sometimes freezes over in the middle of winter, so it should be possible to walk from one country to the other. In truth, this could not really happen for two reasons. First, the two countries are not very friendly towards each other. Second, the strong sea currents mean the ice is not stable enough to cross safely.
texts.4: What is the oldest musical instrument ever found? The answer, believe it or not, is the flute. That does not mean that it was exactly the same as the modern versions. Early flutes were made of animal bones with holes drilled into them. The oldest are thought to be some 43,000 years old. These days, they tend to be made of metal. If you are just starting to learn, you will probably use a nickel or brass one. A musician who plays the flute for a living, however, will actually use one that is made of solid silver or gold.
texts.5: When you learn to swim, you are helping to continue a sport that humans have been doing for centuries. There are cave paintings in Egypt that show people swimming some ten thousand years ago. They appear to be doing the breaststroke although it might be the doggy paddle. Perhaps even more impressive is the fact that these pictures were found in an area of rocky desert. It could not have been easy to find enough water to drink, let alone bathe in. No wonder they thought it was such a special event that they decided to make a record of it.
texts.6: Deep in the heart of the Forest of Fools stood a lonely tower. Few had seen it and lived to tell the tale. Even so, the legend of the warlock’s treasure refused to die. For it was told that the wicked wizard who had built the tower had also discovered the secret to never ending life. Long after any other humans would have faded from memory, he used dark magic to stay young and maintain his strength. Through fair means or foul, he had then used his time to gather a vast amount of wealth which he stored in his dungeon.
texts.7: Do your sentences make sense? If they don’t, consider what the word ‘sentence’ actually means. Its root comes from Latin – the language the Romans used to speak – and is all about having an opinion, a feel or a sense of something. So, each sentence should contain a thought or idea that makes sense. Yes, you can join them together using conjunctions to make longer, more complex sentences. But even then, you should not make them too lengthy as it will become more difficult to make sense of what you are trying to write. Then what would the Romans say?
texts.8: Troy sat on the wall outside the corner shop. Inside, his friends were enjoying the thrill of choosing their sweets. Having only three pence to his name, he knew that there would be nothing that he could afford, so there was no point in even looking. He reached into his pocket and pulled out his feeble collection of coins. Why did they even bother making them if they couldn’t be used to buy anything? He rubbed his thumb over the two pence piece, as if cleaning it up would somehow increase its value. But then something happened that made him rub his own eyes instead.
texts.9: How much would you weigh if you lived on a different planet? Often when we talk about weight, we actually mean mass. After all, mass is what we really measure using kilos and grams. Weight is a force caused by the effect of gravity on a mass. Your mass would be the same whatever planet you were on because it is about you. On the moon, for example, your weight would be less because the effect of the moon’s gravity is much less than Earth’s. Stand on Jupiter, however, and your weight would rocket because its greater size means it has stronger gravity.
texts.10: Soil is extremely important. Without soil, no plants would grow and there would be nothing to eat. So perhaps it would help to have the recipe, just in case we ever ran out. First, you need crunched rocks. These need to be ground into tiny particles, but just how tiny depends upon the type of soil you want. Next you need the rotting remains of dead plants and animals. Yummy! Stir in a healthy dollop of micro-organisms to break it all down. Then mix together using worms and other minibeasts. Finally, leave for a thousand years per inch (2 ½ cm) of soil.
texts.11: Think how much you know about the place where you live. Now think about what it was like before you arrived on the scene. Most of us live in a village, town or city that has been there for centuries. Over the years, there are bound to have been people who have been remembered for doing great things. Do you know who they are? There are usually clues, if you keep your eyes open. Perhaps there is a statue that you have never really given a second glance. Maybe there’s a name that keeps appearing on buildings or street signs.
texts.12: Look at any map of the world and you will notice that the continents of North and South America are joined by a very narrow strip of land. This also separates the Atlantic from the Pacific. Right up until the 19th century, any ship that wanted to travel from one ocean to the other had to go around the southern tip of South America. This would take nearly two weeks and mean sailing through some very rough seas. It was a big problem for world trade. The answer was to build a ship canal right through what we now call Panama.
texts.13: Most of us like a good sing-song, even if we’re not very good. But have you ever wondered how we make the noise that gives us a voice? Inside your neck there is a tube called the larynx through which air passes between your mouth and nose and your lungs. Stretched across the larynx are folded strips of tissue called vocal chords. These move in a way that makes the air vibrate at different speeds. Faster movements make higher notes and slower ones make lower notes. We then need our lips, teeth and tongue to turn the tune into words.
texts.14: Great sports teams will always need great players. But success depends on more than having a group of skilled individuals. The coach needs to look at the pool of talent and choose the ones that will be most likely to work together as a well-balanced team. For example, a cricket team could have all the best bowlers in the world but if they don’t have anyone who can score runs with the bat, they will find it hard to win any game. Also, a netball team could be superb at keeping possession, but what good is that if none of them can score?
texts.15: English is a very rich and special language. Whatever you want to say, there are often many different words you can use. The trick is to find the ones that best express your particular meaning. How did we get the words we use today? Thanks to our eventful history, new words kept being added to the mix from all sorts of different languages. The word bicycle, for example, comes from the Latin for two (bi) and the Greek for circle or wheel.  The result is the name of a machine that no one in the ancient world ever dreamed of.
texts.16: Zara glanced around the room. Someone had tried really hard to make it look calm and relaxing. There were soothing pictures on the walls. Potted plants were dotted around the place. A coffee table covered with magazines tried and failed to suggest that this was an ordinary cosy lounge. But all Zara could think about was her teeth. Had her brushing been thorough enough? Was it a good or bad thing that she hadn’t lost all her baby teeth yet? How many sweets was too many? Just then, the door opened and a lady with a kind smile said, ‘Zara?’
texts.17: Someone must know, surely? I was certain that everyone could see the dark cloud hanging over me. I felt like I was wearing a high-viz jacket of sadness, but if anyone had noticed, they hadn’t cared to show it. No one gave me more than a brief glance as I trudged through the middle of the bus and found a seat at the back, right in the corner. Leaning my head against the window, I used my finger to track the rain drops as they slid down the pane. It was as if I were practising how to follow the right path.
texts.18: At the top of the stairs, Agnes took a deep breath. Why did the master of the house want to see her? She had only been working there a few days – surely, she couldn’t have done anything terribly wrong in such a short time? As she walked down the dimly lit passage, the grumpy old portraits on the wall glared down at her. Even they seemed to be frowning down at her and telling her she was naughty. By the time she had knocked on his door, she was trembling so much that she could hardly hold the handle when she was told to ‘Enter!’

texts.0: What do you get if you add a netball team to a string quartet, a married couple, new-born triplets and a football team? Your first thought might be 'a strange party', but if you want a mathematical answer, you need to dig deeper. That's because they are all completely different from each other. In order to add them together, you should first find something they all have in common – the fact that they are groups of people. Once you know how many are in each group, you're away. The same is true when you add fractions – they all need to share the same common thing, their denominator.
texts.1: Is there anything that frustrates you about writing? Maybe you don't like having to check spellings or meanings in a dictionary. Perhaps you wish that you already had such a great knowledge of words that you didn't need to check a thesaurus to find the one that is most pertinent (it means relevant). You might even dislike having to make notes or plans. But imagine going to visit a professional writer. What do you think you would find? That's right – a dictionary, thesaurus, notes and plans. Like tractors to farmers or thermometers to nurses, those are the tools of the writer's trade.
texts.2: We often hear about the damage that humans cause to the environment. While this is certainly true, we can also have a positive impact. For example, there is a really cool insect that lives in our country called the stag beetle. These beetles are big – nearly eight centimetres long – with fierce looking 'antlers'. If you're lucky, you might see them flying around on warm evenings. Sadly, they are dying out, however, mostly due to the lack of suitable habitat. If you have the space, why not help to protect them by creating a pile of rotten logs where they can lay their eggs?
texts.3: You might believe that the Anglo Saxons are long gone and, to a certain extent, you'd be right. As far as Britain is concerned, their time was really between the eighth and eleventh centuries. But there are still traces where they live on, if you know where to look – including your own address. Many of the place names that are so familiar to us today actually come from Anglo Saxon roots. If your home town's name ends in bury, borough, ton or ley, then the Anglo Saxons started a settlement there. Your next question is, what do these roots mean?
texts.4: If you glance at a map of Britain, with a bit of imagination you might think that it looks like someone sitting down. Scotland is the head; the arms are folded over a very full tummy to make Wales; Devon and Cornwall are the outstretched legs and feet; and East Anglia is, well, what we use to sit on. If that is the case, then the backbone of this craggy figure must be the Pennines – a range of hills, moors and mountains that divides northern England. Large sections of the Pennines are protected as an area of outstanding natural beauty.
texts.5: So, you've found a musical instrument that you want to play; how long it will take for you to become good at it? This question, you won't be surprised to learn, will have various answers. First, it depends on how good you want to be. If you want to play music professionally, you will probably have to practise for thousands of hours to reach the right standard. But remember, music should be a pleasure, and there is nothing wrong with just getting to a level that gives you enjoyment, providing, of course, that it's not too painful for everyone else!
texts.6: For a sport with such an English name, badminton has a long and global history. Once called 'battledore and shuttlecock', it dates right back to early Greece, India and China where it was played some two thousand years ago. The word shuttlecock has stuck as the name of the feathered object that gets hit over a net. The sport itself is named after the big country house in the west of England, where it was enjoyed in the nineteenth century. Even though it was played by the ancient Greeks, it is one of the younger sports at the Olympic Games.
texts.7: Clouds swept over the cold, watchful moon like a cloak shrouding a face. Across the lonely moor, the rising wind started to shake the trees and bushes along the side of the muddy track and unseen animal voices shrieked into the night. Still the coach pressed on, pulled by a tiring team of four anxious horses. Inside, the kindly gentleman softly squeezed his daughter's hand to calm her racing pulse. Meanwhile, less than a mile away, two cruel eyes sprang open, alerted by the sound of approaching hooves. They then narrowed as their owner's mouth stretched into a greedy smile.
texts.8: In a panicky flurry of feathers, Ferdinand launched himself into the air to escape the vicious broomstick. What was wrong with humans? First, they built these wonderful stone cliffs, so perfect for resting and nesting. Then, they got upset whenever he and his fellow pigeons perched on the ledges to relax their wings and unload their droppings. Madness! Not that he had time to worry about that now. Out here in the space between the tower blocks, he was in serious danger from the hawks. Where had they suddenly arrived from and why had his mother not warned him about them?
texts.9: Normally, maths and English stay very separate. But, sometimes, they swing towards each other and briefly come together, like acrobats on the trapeze. In fact, a good example is the word trapeze. This comes from the word trapezium – a four-sided, 2D shape with one pair of parallel lines. The circus act got its name from the outline made by the ropes, bar and roof. It was given that title by Jules Leotard, who we can also thank for that item of clothing. And the funny thing is that the word trapezium first came from the Latin for a bench – not very daring at all!
texts.10: Do you have a favourite author? Perhaps you have more than one. If so, can you explain what it is that you particularly enjoy about their stories? Is it how they describe settings, characters and action with such skill that they capture your interest until the end? Or is it that they are magicians of the unusual, experimenting with language in a way that surprises and delights you? Maybe they just create unforgettable tales. One thing is certain, you couldn't possibly put your hand on your heart and say they are the best authors ever. Why? Because you haven't read them all.
texts.11: Any skilled worker will tell you that you need the right tools for the job and the same holds true when it comes to teeth. Herbivores – plant-eating animals – need strong teeth with flat surfaces for grinding down grass and leaves and, even then, they need special stomachs to digest it all properly. Carnivores – meat eaters – need sharp teeth to slice and rip the flesh from their prey. But what about omnivores like humans that can eat both animals and vegetables? The answer is to have all the tools, which is why we have blunt molars as well as sharp canines and incisors.
texts.12: What would you do if a bunch of vicious thugs kept attacking your villages and towns and stealing your money? It was a real problem for the Anglo Saxons when the Vikings were running riot all over England. Although they did have some success on the battlefield, the Saxons really preferred to live and farm in peace. That is why they decided to pay the Vikings not to raid them through a tax called Danegeld. Although it might seem rather a timid thing to do, either way they would lose their money, but at least they wouldn't lose their lives.
texts.13: Imagine you have been given a totally undiscovered new land and the job of placing ports and harbours around it. Where would you choose? For a start, you'd probably find somewhere that could keep your boats sheltered from the worst storms and roughest waves. If you were clever, you might also think about somewhere inland, so as to reduce the distance your merchants have to transport their goods over the ground. But the sea doesn't go inland, does it? No, but rivers do, so you can see why so many of our biggest ports today are located on wide river estuaries.
texts.14: If you loved music, what would be the worst thing that could happen to you? Ludwig van Beethoven played the piano to the highest standard, conducted whole orchestras and had a gift for composing. So, imagine how terrible it must have been for him when, before he had even reached his thirtieth birthday, he began to lose his hearing. That's like a painter going blind, or a cook losing the senses of taste and smell. Yet even that failed to hold him back. Although he stopped performing, he continued to write music which is still loved and performed around the world today.
texts.15: Sport is supposed to get your heart beating faster. That's one of the ways we can make sure that our bodies stay fit and healthy. But there is more than one way to get your chest pounding, and they don't all involve running around getting sweaty. More and more, we are beginning to understand the benefit of adventurous activities. These introduce you to new, exciting experiences. They test your courage and help you to push yourself to new extremes. And whether you find yourself crawling through mud or scaling great heights, they're bound to set your pulse racing.
texts.16: He knew he should have taken it to the police. In fact, he probably should have left it where he'd found it and alerted the bus driver – you couldn't be too careful these days. Even so, Hashim simply couldn't resist sliding the zip and having a look inside. There, he found a slim, shiny laptop. Glancing around to see if anyone was watching, he opened the lid and was surprised to see that the screen was on, revealing a desktop covered with icons. That was unusual – not even a log-in screen. Suddenly a speech bubble appeared bearing the words, "Greetings Hashim!"
texts.17: No one could quite remember when they had first noticed she was there. It was as if she had appeared by magic. But then, people started to ask questions about the strange woman sitting on the bench in the middle of the traffic island. Unable to find the answers they were seeking, the busy-bodies of the village increased the number of reasons for taking a stroll. Of course, they said that they needed the exercise, or had run out of potatoes, or something. Anything to walk past the stranger without having the good manners to stop and talk to her.
texts.18: This was only the second occasion in her life that Tamsin had attempted to play tennis. Trying to forget how it had ended last time, she picked up the racket and hit it against her hand. The strings were surprisingly hard and left a pattern of square marks on her skin. 'Ready?' called Jamila from the opposite side of the row of chairs they were using as a net. Tamsin nodded and bent down like she had seen the professional players do on the telly. When the ball approached, she swung her arm, then watched in dismay as the ball disappeared over the fence.

texts.0: No doubt, you recognise the term ‘prime number’. You might also know that it means any whole number that is greater than one but has no factors other than one and itself. You might not immediately view this to be a hugely interesting property, but it is an idea that has gripped maths experts for many years. Ancient Egyptian writings have been found that hint at some sort of knowledge of them. However, the first people to study them for definite were the Greeks, over two thousand years ago. They even proved that there is no limit to how many prime numbers there are.
texts.1: Now that you are able to read, you might want to think about what you are reading. Of course, the ability to read well and quickly is especially important when it comes to doing research. But don’t forget that reading should also be a pleasure. From myths and legends to modern day fiction, there are so many excellent stories to entertain and delight you. Not every book will be your cup of tea, so it’s fine if you favour a particular type of story. Just remember that a lot of thought has gone into writing it, so enjoy every word.
texts.2: When you carry out a science experiment, you often need to measure something, such as weight or temperature. After all, the whole purpose tends to involve asking a question, then finding a way to gauge any changes you notice. That doesn’t mean you will achieve the same results every time. That is why scientists recommend repeating your tests in order to get a range of results. Some of these you might suspect are mistakes because they are nothing like the rest. It sometimes helps to find an average of the remaining values. That might give you a truer picture of what has happened.
texts.3: Sometimes, historical events get retold in such a way that they end up giving completely the wrong impression. A good example is the story of King Cnut, who is often also called Canute. According to his myth, he sat beside the sea and ordered the tide not to come in, but ended up damp and embarrassed. In truth, however, Cnut was a very wise leader who was fed up with his people telling him how marvellous he was. Getting his feet wet at the seaside was his way of proving that he couldn’t really tell the oceans what to do.
texts.4: When you think of the harm and chaos that volcanos cause, you might think about big blasts and flying rocks. You might know that red-hot lava can pour down the side of the mountain, burning everything in its path and crushing communities. You might have even read about how the people of Pompeii in ancient Rome could not escape the deadly ash and gasses. But did you know that the impact of a volcano can be felt for hundreds if not thousands of miles? When one erupted in Iceland in 2010, the smoke grounded aircraft for weeks across much of Europe.
texts.5: Which musical family do you think the piano belongs to: percussion, brass, string or woodwind? If you look inside one, you will find a row of strings. These are easiest to see in a grand or baby grand piano than an upright version, especially when the lid has been raised. Percussion means hitting or striking, and there are little hammers that strike the strings to make the notes when you press the keys. Even so, it is still the strings that make the sound. Perhaps that is why it is sometimes considered to be part of both families – or maybe neither!
texts.6: Can you guess what was the first recorded sporting competition between two countries? Although it is not always easy to be certain, there is one individual event that lays claim to that title. If you assume that the original Olympics only involved the people from one country, ancient Greece, you have to skip forward to 1844. Believe it or not, this was when a team from the United States played a team from Canada in the centre of what is now New York. And what was the sport? You might be very surprised to learn that it was cricket.
texts.7: By the third day, Tomaz was beginning to get concerned. Every day he would walk past the front door and windows of their neighbour, Mrs Watson, and every day she would wave cheerfully from her chair. But he hadn’t seen her all week and it was now Wednesday. At first, his mother said that she didn’t want to interfere – she was probably visiting relatives or something. Finally, Tomaz managed to persuade her to have a look, if only to stop him bothering her. When she peered through the window, Mum gasped and reached for her mobile – there was Mrs Watson, slumped on the sofa and she didn’t appear conscious.
texts.8: Dora felt sick to the pit of her stomach. She had been saving for that bicycle for a whole year, but now she found that she was forty pounds short. How could that have occurred? Through all her saving, sacrifice and jobs for Grannie, it had remained the same price for eleven months. Why did they have to increase it now, in the twelfth month, just as she had thought she had achieved her dream? According to the shop assistant, they had only put it up the previous day. He tried to recommend a different, cheaper one, but Dora wasn’t interested.
texts.9: Dora felt sick to the pit of her stomach. She had been saving for that bicycle for a whole year, but now she found that she was forty pounds short. How could that have occurred? Through all her saving, sacrifice and jobs for Grannie, it had remained the same price for eleven months. Why did they have to increase it now, in the twelfth month, just as she had thought she had achieved her dream. According to the shop assistant, they had only put it up the previous day. He tried to recommend a different, cheaper one, but Dora wasn’t interested.
texts.10: This was disastrous! On first hearing about the new housing estate, they thought it would be a good thing for the area. But when they learnt where they were planning to build it, there was uproar. How could they even consider using the land by the brook? It was the only natural environment they had and everyone knew that it was home to rare wildlife. They thought about writing to the government, but someone pointed out that they wouldn’t interfere. When the local council refused to get involved either, they knew that they would have to do something about it themselves.
texts.11: Maths frequently uses words in its own special way. Take, for example, the words ‘proper’ and ‘improper’. When used in everyday language, they can feel like being criticised, especially when talking about behaviour. If someone told you that your actions were improper, you might feel a bit awkward or that you were being told off. But when it comes to fractions, it only indicates that the top number is greater than the lower one. That means it’s worth more than one whole. But that’s easily solved by converting it into a mixed number. All you need to do is find out how.
texts.12: The better you get at reading fiction, the more interesting it becomes because authors start playing games with you. Stories for younger readers tend to be rather straightforward. But more advanced writing recognises that you are grown up enough to work out what is not immediately apparent. Although you might not always be conscious of it, you start to fill in the gaps. But be warned – authors are like magicians: they only let you see what they want you to see. So next time you read a book, see if you can spot how your viewpoint is being directed.
texts.13: In many ways, the lifecycle of salmon follows a familiar pattern. The adult females lay eggs, the eggs hatch, the young grow into adults and so on. But it is what happens in between hatching and laying that is so remarkable for North American salmon. Theirs is a tale of extreme physical effort. The newly hatched young spend a few months in fresh water streams. Then they head out into the ocean. After around eight years at sea, they follow their noses back to the same stream in which they were born. However, they do have to leap waterfalls and dodge predators along the way.
texts.14: The dawn of steam power was more than just a great step forward in technology: it had a huge and lasting effect on the culture of our nation too. Until the Victorian age, travel between Britain’s towns and cities was very hard. As the rail network grew, however, it became much easier and cheaper to move around the country. People from different regions began to mix more often, changing the way they viewed each other. Families could afford to go on holiday. It also meant that diets could be more healthy as fresh food could get to market before it went off.
texts.15: If you were asked to name some European countries, you would probably be able to mention the larger ones such as England or Germany. But did you know that Europe also has a number of very small states? Some are so tiny that you might not even be aware of their existence. Look on a map showing physical features and you will see that between France and Spain is a range of mountains call the Pyrenees. Tucked in amongst those peaks is the minute country of Andorra. To get from one end of the country to the other is a forty kilometre drive.
texts.16: When thinking about the rhythm of music, it is often easy to get confused with the beat. Beat really refers to the steady pulse of the music. It’s a bit like a sentence in which there is just one syllable in each word. For example, ‘I want to go to the beach,’ has seven beats. Rhythm is still a regular, repeating pattern, but can have more variety within the sequence. For example, ‘Danny doesn’t want to wiggle his toes’ also has seven beats, if you read each word as a beat, but can you hear the difference in the rhythm?
texts.17: Although it doesn’t have quite the fame or money as sports such as football, golf and cycling, hockey is enjoyed by men and women all around the world. What’s more, it probably has a longer history than most. Images of a variety of games that involve hitting objects with sticks have been found in cultures from the Aztecs to the Greeks. The earliest record, however, comes from ancient Egypt. But that might just be because they were especially good at preserving accounts of their lives. As often seems the case, though, it was the British who shaped the modern game.
texts.18: Kayla wondered why she had agreed to sacrifice her free time for this. But somehow she had managed to let Jen persuade her to sneak out while her parents were busy entertaining friends. ‘It’ll be really cool,’ babbled her friend as they approached the old cemetery. Kayla sincerely hoped so, but at the moment she was feeling more cold than cool. Freezing, in fact – the late October air was turning her breath into ghostly clouds. Not that she believed in such spooky nonsense, and the idea of walking through a graveyard at night filled her more with curiosity than fear.
texts.19: A stern looking security guard signalled for their car to stop. What was going on? They were only on their way to the leisure centre for a swim. A soldier stepped up to the driver’s window, crouched down and had a good look inside. ‘What is the purpose of your visit?’ he growled. When Dad replied, ‘Exercise,’ the soldier asked whether they had any proof of identity. When Mum enquired why they would need it, the soldier snarled that the President had declared all water to be the property of the state and its use, especially for swimming, was to be strictly controlled.

texts.0: For centuries, mankind has found it useful to divide up the world using the ideas of longitude and latitude. These are imaginary lines that circle the world in an east-west direction for latitude and a north-south direction for longitude. The most well-known lines of latitude are the equator, which marks a line of equal distance between the two poles, and the tropic of Cancer and the tropic of Capricorn, which are 23.5⁰ north and 23.5⁰ south respectively. These were easy to establish by noting the position of the sun at midday. Longitude was more difficult to measure, yet extremely important because ships needed to know exactly where they were. Even small mistakes could lead to shipwrecks.
texts.1: This was it! Surely, this was where the hoard had been hidden. With mounting excitement, they clawed away at the soil on the ground directly below the portrait of Count Vasser. Soon their fingers found a square slab about half a metre across. As they blew away the remaining dirt, an inscription was revealed, carved into the stone. ‘To the thieves that seek to steal what is mine, remember this: when it comes to gold and jewels, nothing is beneath me!’ But the men simply laughed. They were not daunted by threats and curses from centuries ago. Using an iron bar as a lever, they carefully lifted the heavy trap door.
texts.2: The period before the Romans arrived in Britain is known as the Iron Age. The people who lived here – the Celts – had learnt how to make tools and weapons out of iron, which meant that farming was easier and warfare was even more dangerous. The Celts began to live together in larger settlements so that people with different skills – potters, weavers, carpenters and blacksmiths – could all contribute to the smooth working of the village. To protect themselves, they built well-defended enclosures of ditches and walls which have become known as hill forts, even though they are not all on hills. Their earthworks can still be seen in many sites across the UK today.
texts.3: There was a sudden rush of icy air as the door was opened. Standing at the front of the queue, Morgan was able to look down at the dark shapes far below; just the occasional pinprick of yellow light betraying the location of a house. Suddenly, he heard a voice yelling in his ear, ‘Go, go, go!’ and a sharp push propelled him out into mid-air. As the ground rushed up to meet him, he counted slowly to ten, then pulled the cord. With a jolt, the parachute opened, the roar of the wind and engines faded, and he began to drift downwards in near silence.
texts.4: What do you see when a kettle is boiling? Your first instinct might be to say ‘steam’, but you would not be right. Strictly speaking, steam – the gas or vapour caused by the evaporation of water – is invisible. The white clouds you see coming out of a kettle, or drifting across the sky for that matter, are actually tiny droplets of water which have condensed from the gaseous form into liquid but are too small to be affected by gravity. As often happens, there is a difference between scientific explanations and common understanding. As a scientist, it is important to know that water vapour is invisible, but to say that you can’t see steam rising from a kettle might just be annoying.
texts.5: Any violent shaking of the earth’s surface is alarming as we have come to expect the ground to be solid and stable. There can be natural causes such as landslides or even man-made ones such as explosions. Perhaps the most destructive and terrifying, however, are earthquakes. They can have a number of different possible causes, but the most common is the shifting of the planet’s surface along its fault lines. This is because the earth’s crust is not made up of one single shell, but a jigsaw of massive areas of land known as ‘tectonic plates’. Where these meet, there is some scope for movement, and even the slightest shift can release an enormous amount of energy – enough to shake whole cities to the ground.
texts.6: What was that? Phoebe had definitely heard a noise. For a moment, she lay rigid with her head on the pillow, staring at the ceiling. There it was again – a short, harsh squeaking noise, like a chair being scraped across a tiled floor. She tiptoed over to her bedroom door and silently opened it a fraction, hoping to get a better idea of what the noise was. For a few moments, the only sound she could hear was her own heavy breathing. Then there came a loud grunt from her parents’ bedroom followed by a deep sigh as Dad rolled over and resumed snoring.
texts.7: As human activity changes over the centuries, so does the size of its settlements. This is as true around the world as it is in the United Kingdom. In England, London has been the largest city since the Norman conquest in 1066. Meanwhile, other places have risen or fallen in the rankings depending on how people’s jobs have changed. For example, some 700 years ago, farming and sea trade were really important, so places like Bristol, King’s Lynn, Lincoln and Norwich were amongst the largest in the country. Fast-forward a few hundred years and the scene looked very different. Huge new factories and mills drew people in from the fields. That meant that places like Manchester and Birmingham rapidly grew to become amongst the top five cities by population in England.
texts.8: There are moments in history when the future of a whole nation hangs in the balance. Just such a moment happened in 1940 when Britain stood alone against the might of Nazi Germany under its leader Adolf Hitler. Hitler never really wanted to invade Britain, but he also could not afford to leave it alone, so he ordered his air force, the Luftwaffe, to destroy the Royal Air Force (RAF). This would make it much easier for his armies to cross the English Channel and take over the whole country. He hadn’t counted on the bravery and determination of the young fighter pilots from Britain and her allies to beat back the massed attacks by the German aircraft.
texts.9: Jamal checked his watch again, then quickened his pace. His train was due in four minutes and he reckoned he was about four minutes’ walk to the station. Anyway, these days they were always late – that’s what his dad kept saying when he was grumbling about his day. Still, he absolutely had to catch this one, otherwise he would be in big trouble. Bee-baaarb! The unmistakable sound of the train’s horn made him jump. It was early! He broke into a run, but almost immediately heard a slap on the pavement behind him. His wallet! No money – just his ticket. But if he stopped, he’d surely miss the train.
texts.10: To make anything move, you need a force. But, unless you are in a total vacuum, such as outer space, you will immediately encounter resistance. Air resistance is a form of friction between a moving object and the molecules that make up air. Water resistance is a similar force between an object and water molecules, without which we would not be able to swim. Even though it feels like we can just dip our hands in to a bowl of water without meeting any resistance, as soon as we pull back our hands, there is clearly a force working against us. Cup your hands as you pull them back, and you can increase the resistance, which means you can push the rest of your body through the water.
texts.11: We all know that even the mightiest rivers start as a little trickle. Rain falls on the high ground and most of it soaks into the soil, which acts like a gigantic sponge. Some of it does find its way out to the surface through springs. As the stream is joined by others, known as tributaries, the main river grows in size and power until it finally reaches the sea. At 220 miles, the Severn is the UK’s longest river and has its source 610 metres above sea level. However, the source of the second longest, the Thames (just five miles shorter than the Severn), is located only 110 metres above sea level. Nearly every other major river in the British Isles starts at a higher point. Clearly, the height of the source has no bearing on the length of the river.
texts.12: The reign of Queen Victoria is often seen as a golden age of progress for the United Kingdom. The vastness of the British Empire meant that it was a time of great opportunity and many people became very wealthy as a result. Not everyone was so fortunate, however. Within the country’s rapidly expanding cities, families were crowded together in very cramped accommodation which were excellent breeding grounds for disease. What’s more, even though the cities offered plenty of work, those jobs were often dangerous. As a result, people were lucky if they managed to live to see their 50s.
texts.13: With a secret smile, Lily picked it up and turned it over and over in her hands. For as long as she could remember, she had been enchanted by her grandmother’s musical box. Whenever they visited, she always found an excuse to sneak a look, even though she knew it was strictly forbidden to go into Nana’s bedroom. Unable to resist any longer, she twisted the metal key and opened the lid. The familiar tinkle of the tune started playing immediately but there was something wrong with the little dancer. Normally, she twirled around in time with the music. Today, she just sat in the middle of the box, arms folded, legs crossed, turning her back on Lily.
texts.14: Science is about finding answers to questions about the world around us. To do this, we usually devise experiments designed to reveal results and patterns that help us to make sense of what we are looking at. The trick is to make sure that your investigation is actually doing what you want it to. This might seem like a strange point to make – after all, you should know what you are trying to find out. However, any number of factors could be causing an effect. These factors are known as variables. In order to be able to trust our findings, we need to make sure that we have controlled all variables except the one we are investigating.
texts.15: Beside a tall, mossy tree, she paused for a moment, chest heaving, as she leaned with one hand against the gnarled bark. Absent-mindedly looking down, past the sodden legs of her combats, she spied something that raised her flagging spirits. A twig had been squashed into the soft earth. When she crouched down to inspect, she noticed a couple of silvery hairs sticking to her fingers. On examining the tree trunk more closely, she saw that it was festooned with pale, glistening fur. She was getting closer. She just had to make sure she caught up with her quarry before the hunters.
texts.16: He left the headteacher’s office as quickly as he could, her piercing words still reverberating around his mind. He should have gone outside for break but instead he sought the sanctuary of the classroom. He could hardly have been in more trouble so what difference would one more broken rule make? Anyway, Mr Corrigan was out on duty so he knew he would be alone. Eventually, his breathing returned to normal and he wiped his eyes with his sleeve. Now what? No one believed him, yet he had a clear conscience and was determined to prove his innocence.
texts.17: Once again, the slamming of the door was followed by the clunk of the key turning in the lock. Maude stared miserably at the hunk of bread and wedge of cheese. Even though she was ravenous, she resisted the temptation to scrape off the layer of blue-green mould and bolt it down – after all, there would be nothing else until the same time tomorrow. Instead, she tried to distract herself by looking into the full-length mirror on the wardrobe, partly to confirm her existence, partly to imagine how she might have looked had she been born into a happier household.
texts.18: Well, this was awkward! Jess shifted in her seat, edging as far as possible from the suited man snoring next to her. She could just about see the sleeve of Mum’s coat a little way down the aisle. Between them sat dozens of strangers, all packed into the same carriage yet desperate to ignore each other by any means possible – phone, laptop, newspaper, sleep. If only they could have taken a later one, they would have been able to sit together. Jess tried to guess where her neighbouring passengers worked: bank, bank, office, government, office, secretary, bank. What job could possibly be worth this?
texts.19: The grown-ups were talking. Tuning out the incessant drone, Ibra’s eyes swept lazily around his uncle’s room. On top of a tall cupboard, in the dingiest corner, sat a battered, bulging, brown bag … a bag that was alive! Yes, he was sure of it – one of the bulges had moved. And another. He glanced at his relatives but they were all engaged in an intense discussion. No interruption would be tolerated unless it was very important. But how important was a living hold-all? Especially one that had now sprouted the head of a snake, which Ibra instantly recognised to be some sort of python.
texts.20: A large crowd had gathered along the roadside. Lotte kept a firm hold on her mother’s hand. Too large to sit on her shoulders, she squeezed herself towards the front in order to get a good view. First, came the motorcycles, followed by open-topped cars carrying stern-looking men with peaked caps. Finally, it was the turn of the steel-headed soldiers. Lotte heard them before she could see them: the crunching rhythm of boots on stone announcing their arrival in the main square. No one cheered. No flags waved. Most of the townsfolk just stared impassively at the invasion of the uninvited.
texts.21: Not daring to switch on the light, she crept from the bedroom, taking great care to avoid the creaking floor board, which refused to be silenced, despite her DIY attempts. A sliver of light escaped from underneath the bathroom door, piercing the darkness which consumed the landing. Fighting the urge to retreat to the sanctuary of her own warm bed, she tiptoed further. With a touch as soft as the silk scarf her mother once wore, something or someone brushed against her bare leg.  A shriek, that she could only assume came from her own trembling throat, shattered the silence as she raced to her room, slamming the door behind her with a ferocious bang.
texts.22: The familiar bile rose in her throat. She fought it down and attempted to take a deep breath (as her mother had advised many times) but the same, searing pain in her chest returned. The cacophony of noise in the dining hall assaulted her; it rained painful blows on her head, her ears, her mind. She had hoped getting through her first morning, at her new school, would be the hardest part but she was to be disappointed. Rows of chattering, shouting, shoving students spread in front of her. She stood, frozen to the spot (aside from the involuntary shaking in her hands) as she gripped the food tray with white knuckles. Gravy spilled from her plate and pooled in the corner of the tray, threatening to escape over the edge and onto her new, conspicuously shiny shoes. Her dad, having incessantly polished them whilst having his morning coffee, proudly announced she could eat her dinner off them. Sighing at the irony, she once again focused on taking that deep breath.
texts.23: John anxiously shuffled his feet, cramped into new shoes, then inched his way to the door of the cool, dark space within. He could see his sister’s hat protruding over the top of the guests’ heads, at least ten rows in front of him. He was relieved he didn’t have to sit with her in that excruciatingly embarrassing outfit. All around him grew flowers he recognised from his parent’s garden– roses, lilies, geraniums. If only he could escape their pervasive, cloying scent. He tried to work out how much longer the seemingly endless ceremony would take. He knew he couldn’t leave before the end but the relentless itch in his eyes and the intolerable urge to sneeze was more than he could take. He couldn’t understand why anyone would choose to do this outside when there was a conference room, air-conditioned and comfortable, right inside.
texts.24: Left with nothing, Evelyn had no choice but to risk the deadly voyage and emigrate to America. The ‘Land of Opportunity’ her sister had called it, when she sent a letter begging her to follow her there, promising Evelyn a job and a home.  Determinedly, Evelyn boarded the ‘coffin’ ship with a sack, containing only a loaf of bread and salted fish. The two small coins her grandmother had pressed into her hand as she left were sewed into the lining of her dress. Concerned for her grandmother, she initially refused to accept them but eventually relented, knowing that without them she had little chance of survival. As she squeezed into the tiny cot in the bowels of the ship, her mouth watered thinking of the bread and fish in her sack. Calculating the length of the voyage, she knew she could only have a bite a day if she were to have enough for the whole journey.
texts.25: Sara pedalled, not daring to look back. The sun scorched relentlessly onto the back of her neck. They had called it ‘the race of the year’ and they weren’t wrong! As she flew down the hill, she felt that same exhilarating rush that she only ever felt when on the road. She was in the lead but sensed from experience that her competitors weren’t far behind and she couldn’t lose. Not again. Drowning out these thoughts of self-doubt, she pushed the pedals with all her might, feeling every muscle strain and scream with the effort.  With the quickest of glances, she glimpsed the finish line and the crowds of spectators with their flags and garishly bright homemade banners. Head down, determinedly pushing herself over the last few metres, she failed to see the rock protruding from the ground.
texts.26: The wait is over. With a flourish, the ringmaster announces with his large booming voice, that the show is about to commence. A spotlight rotates from the ringmaster and rises to the pinnacle of the big, blue top.  Our eyes follow. With gasps echoing around the tent, we watch open-mouthed as a woman, in a resplendent, sparkling dress, balances on top of a platform. She stands high above our heads. Without warning, she lunges gracefully through the air as if diving into a ocean. Light scatters across the tent, as she serenely navigates towards an unseen destination, in this apparent abyss of emptiness.  I instinctively grab my mother’s arm. The older members of the audience cover their eyes. They are too fearful to see the outcome. The youngsters sit rooted to the spot, eyes open like saucers, as they stare at this flying spectacle.
